blogs.title: Legatics joins Legora’s integration ecosystem, giving Legora read and write access to live deals
blogs.description: Lawyers using Legora can now ask questions of their live transactions in Legatics and create or update checklists, trackers and issues lists from the work they do in Legora, with each firm’s permissions applied.
blogs.content: Legatics , the transaction management platform used by leading law firms around the world, today announced that it has joined Legora’s product integration ecosystem . The integration connects Legatics to Legora , so lawyers working in Legora can see the current state of their deals in Legatics and make changes to them without switching between the two. Legora is the agentic operating system for legal work. Many of those lawyers are using it for review and drafting on the same complex transactions they are running in Legatics. The information about those transactions, such as what is outstanding, who is responsible for it, what has been signed and what has changed, sits in Legatics. Connecting the two means the Legora Agent can work from that information directly and put the results of its work back onto the deal, where the rest of the deal team, the client and the other side can see it and act on it. What the integration does Ask questions of the live deal. Legora can read matter data held in Legatics, including the status of checklists and trackers, who is responsible for each item, parties, deadlines, comments left by the deal team, and the contents of data rooms and closing binders. A lawyer can ask where a single deal stands or which of their matters need attention this week, and the answer comes from Legatics as it is at that moment. This makes routine reporting much quicker. An associate asked by a partner or client for a status update can have Legora pull the open items, owners and latest comments from Legatics and draft the update in minutes. Update live deals in Legatics, directly from Legora. Legora can also create and update content in Legatics. For example, a lawyer can do the following directly on Legora: review a facility agreement in Legora and create a conditions precedent checklist in Legatics from the Conditions Precedent schedule update the status of checklist items in Legatics as documents are reviewed in Legora record follow-ups from a document review in Legora on a Legatics list, with owners and deadlines build a closing checklist, issues list or documents list in a Legatics matter, with the right columns and starter rows Once that content is in Legatics, it is tracked like everything else on the deal, so the next time someone asks where things stand, the answer is updated to reflect work done in Legora. Legora can only see or change what the individual user can already see or change in Legatics. Write access is optional and is switched on by the firm. Every change made through the integration is recorded in the matter’s audit trail, and administrators can turn the connection off at any time. The integration is available to all mutual customers at no additional cost. “Lawyers want their AI tools to work from the deal as it actually stands, and then do something useful with what they find. Being able to read from Legatics is helpful, but being able to write back to it is what moves a transaction forward. Legora Agent can now do both, under the same permissions firms already rely on for everyone working on the matter,” said Anthony Seale, Founder and CEO of Legatics. “This came directly from our mutual customers. Their lawyers are doing more and more of their analysis and drafting in Legora, but the deal itself is run in Legatics, and copying work from one to the other by hand costs time and means things get missed. We think of Legatics as the infrastructure transactions run on, whether the work is done by a person or an agent, and connecting it to Legora with read and write from the start is an important part of that,” said Rob MacAdam, Chief Product & Strategy Officer at Legatics. “AI is most useful on a transaction when it knows where the deal really stands. blogs.title: How Skills and subagents work together in Legora
blogs.author: Tom Davies
blogs.description: Skills bring your team
blogs.content: Legal work draws on several kinds of expertise at once. When reviewing an agreement, a lawyer applies legal knowledge alongside the team’s review method, the client’s negotiating positions, and drafting conventions. Those inputs inform one another, and all need to be considered in the wider context of the work being done. Skills help the Legora Agent work in a similar way. They allow legal teams to capture and deploy their standards and processes as reusable instructions and supporting materials for the Agent. Skills are modular: the Agent can call on a research methodology, report drafting guidelines, and a client communication style as needed, combining them to carry out an assignment. Some parts of legal work benefit from separate execution. Legora uses subagents where that separation helps, including parallel investigations in legal research . Skills equip the Agent with reusable expertise; subagents allow it to delegate parts of an assignment. Adding expertise and dividing work are different design decisions. Applying team standards with Skills A team might create a Skill for its agreement-review process, another for client-specific guidance, and a third for drafting conventions. Each can be maintained separately and reused across assignments. The Agent applies those Skills together during a review. The review instructions guide what to examine, the client’s negotiating positions inform the recommendation, and the drafting conventions shape how it is expressed. This modularity allows the same drafting Skill to support an agreement review, a research report, or a client update. Teams can refine each body of guidance independently and combine it with others as the assignment requires. Applying another area of expertise does not, by itself, require a separate worker. Using subagents where they improve the outcome Some assignments benefit from dividing work. A legal research question spanning several jurisdictions, for example, can be broken into separate investigations that proceed in parallel. Legora uses subagents for this kind of research. Each receives a task and relevant context, then returns focused findings for the Agent to bring into the wider analysis. A separate working context can also keep extensive intermediate research from overwhelming the main analysis. Choosing when to delegate Asking a colleague to investigate a separate jurisdiction can be a sensible division of work. Asking another colleague to take over a review solely to apply a writing style introduces a handoff for something the reviewing lawyer could apply directly. In either case, delegation requires a brief and a way to incorporate the returned work. The same considerations apply to agents. Each subagent needs enough context to carry out its task, and its findings must be incorporated into the wider analysis. These steps can require additional model calls and tokens. If relevant information is omitted from the brief or the findings returned, the quality of the completed work can also suffer. Legora evaluates whether the benefits of separate execution justify the coordination it requires. We assess the complete assignment: the quality of the answer, how long it takes, the resources it uses, and how much review and correction it requires. Skills and subagents give us complementary ways to improve that result. Expertise can be specialized and reused without requiring a separate worker for every specialty. Where independent execution adds value, the Agent can delegate. Our approach is to apply expertise within the ongoing work and introduce a separate worker when doing so improves the outcome. blogs.title: Legal work, without limits
blogs.description: Legora is the collaborative AI powering lawyers to review and research faster, draft smarter, and advise with precision. Legora adapts to your ways of working, unlocking team and machine collaboration at scale.
blogs.content: Every in-house team has work it would take on with more capacity. A policy that needs updating. Agreements that deserve a closer look. A product initiative that would benefit from legal advice before a line of code is written. Instead, teams have had to make trade-offs. For years, the time needed to complete a task, or cost of engaging with outside counsel have constrained what legal teams can achieve. Then there are the systems and software lawyers use to do the work. Legal intake is tracked in a spreadsheet, contracts live in another tool, spend in a third. Each tool imposes its own limitations on how the work should be executed and managed. AI is beginning to change that equation. As more work becomes feasible, legal teams have an opportunity to rethink how the work is done, where they can deliver even more business value and how they should organize themselves to deliver it. At Legora, we call that ambition legal work, without limits : helping legal teams take on work that was previously out of reach, and shape it around how the team actually works instead of the limits of each tool. When more legal work becomes possible Much of the discussion about legal AI starts with time savings. Those gains matter but their broader significance is what they make worth doing. If reviewing an agreement takes less time, a team can examine a larger share of its contracts. If approved policy guidance becomes easier to access, colleagues can get help at the point of making a decision. If monitoring regulations requires less manual work, a periodic exercise could become a more regular part of how the business manages change. Our view is that legal will experience a version of Jevons’ Paradox: as the cost of doing work falls, demand for it grows. Lower costs, shorter waits and easier access will encourage businesses to seek more legal support. AI adoption across other functions will also accelerate business activity. As the business moves faster, legal teams have an opportunity to bring their expertise to more business-critical decisions as strategic partners. Capturing that opportunity depends on whether in-house teams can move to AI-native ways of working. Learnings from software engineering Software engineering gives us an early indication of where legal work is heading. At Legora, coding agents increasingly complete substantial pieces of work, and we are seeing huge productivity gains per engineer. Internal data shows that between July and October 2026, our engineers have more than tripled the number of code changes shipped to production. We expect legal to follow a similar trajectory as the capabilities needed for legal work mature. Our recent in-house ROI report points the same way, with 80% of participants reporting that they are accomplishing more in the same amount of time when using Legora, with 77% reallocating that saved time to higher-value legal analysis, strategy and complex judgment calls. However, faster output will expose new bottlenecks. Writing code has accelerated faster than human review and the bottleneck modern engineering teams face is in the review process. Legal teams will encounter a similar challenge. If AI produces more drafts, analyses and answers, but each requires the same amount of lawyer attention, work will get stuck in the review queue. The answer is not more reviewers. It is deciding which work needs which kind of review, building confidence and trust in the work that should not need a lawyer in the loop, and creating systems that let lawyers apply their expertise and judgment where required. That makes the next stage of adoption an organizational question, as well as a technological one. A shift to an AI-native operating model We observe three types of operating models within in-house legal today. Manual: Every task requires human initiation, execution, and review. I saw first-hand how the pressures on government were growing: the explosion of evidence in criminal cases, the rise in cases coming through our courts, and an overstretched prison system. In government, we were looking to technology to bring new answers to old problems. In the NHS, for example, da Vinci robotic-assisted surgery was helping patients with prostate cancer, and predictive analysis was being used to bring down waiting lists. blogs.title: What to Check in a Data Processing Agreement Before Procurement Signs Off

blogs.description: Review a vendor DPA before Procurement signs. Check required terms, security, breach notification, subprocessors, transfers, and which issues need escalation.
blogs.content: Insights What to Check in a Data Processing Agreement Before Procurement Signs Off by Harvey Team • Nov 18, 2026 A data processing agreement (DPA) sets the contractual rules for how a vendor processes personal data on another organization’s behalf. Procurement may have agreed on the price and service levels, but the DPA still needs a separate check. What data will the supplier handle? Can it use that data for anything else? What happens if a breach or compliance request comes in? However, a DPA can contain every expected heading and still leave the organization exposed. Before signature, your legal department needs to confirm that the document reflects the actual processing arrangement, includes the protections required by applicable law, and sends any material deviation from approved standards to the person authorized to decide it. Here’s what to check before procurement moves forward. When is a Data Processing Agreement Required? Under Article 28 of the GDPR , a controller engaging a processor to handle personal data on its behalf needs to put a binding processing contract or other legal act in place. The controller determines why and how personal data will be processed and the processor acts on the controller’s instructions. The Irish Data Protection Commission’s guidance makes it clear that the agreement must identify the processing and include specific contractual duties, not just a general promise to comply with privacy law. The need for a particular agreement depends on the parties’ actual roles and the laws or jurisdictions that apply. For example, a vendor might be a processor for the service it provides and an independent controller for a separate activity. U.S. rules can also require specific vendor terms, such as California’s CCPA regulations , which prescribe contractual restrictions and specified business purposes for service providers and contractors. Those provisions aren't the same as GDPR Article 28 mentioned above. Additionally, a nondisclosure agreement protects confidential information but does not replace a required DPA. Likewise, standard contractual clauses used for international data transfers address a different legal question and may be required on top of processor terms. Check What the Vendor Will Actually Process Before Reviewing the Clauses Start with the processing annex and the business’s intended use, not the vendor’s liability cap. The most polished DPA isn’t very useful if its description of the service is wrong. Compare the agreement and its schedules with the order form, statement of work, vendor questionnaire, and what the business sponsor has actually asked the vendor to do. Information to verify Check against Why it matters Purpose, services, and duration Processing annex, order form, SOW It defines scope and permitted use Personal data and affected individuals Data inventory, intake questionnaire It surfaces sensitivity and exposure Contracting parties and roles DPA definitions, entity list It clarifies who gives instructions Storage, support, and access locations Hosting map, security documentation It identifies transfer and access risks Subprocessors and onward processing Current subprocessor list, service diagram It enables authorization and oversight For example, a DPA that only refers to business contact details needs another look if the deployment will give the vendor access to customer records or employee files. Update the description and risk assessment before debating narrower drafting points because the rest of the review depends on getting these facts right. Eight DPA Provisions Legal Should Review Before Sign-Off For each provision, ask three things: Does it meet the applicable legal requirement? Does it match the organization’s approved position? blogs.content: Two years into my career as a disputes lawyer at a leading City firm, I asked myself a question that changed everything: what makes a successful partner in ten years' time? The answer is not more billable hours, a narrower specialism, or a bigger contacts book. The successful partners of the future will be those who have learned to leverage technology so completely that it has fundamentally altered who they are as lawyers - not just the speed at which they work, but the quality of their thinking, the breadth of what they can take on, and the value they deliver to clients. I realised that the lawyers who would thrive were not the ones dabbling in AI. The lawyers who would thrive were rebuilding their entire practice around it. That realisation set me on a path from practising law to helping build the technology I'd become obsessed with. But this piece isn't about me. It's about you - and the mental model shift that will separate the lawyers who thrive in 2030 from those who get left behind. Use cases are just the beginning As a Legal Engineer, a large part of my role involves running use case discovery sessions with the lawyers who use the Legora platform. The objective is straightforward: diagnose friction points in a lawyer's practice, identify which ones AI can address, and build solutions accordingly. These sessions are truly valuable. They give lawyers who are new to AI a concrete starting point, a reason to engage, and real momentum. But here's what I've observed: for many lawyers, use cases become the ceiling rather than the floor. They attend a session, compile a list of four or five things the tool is good for, and then reach for AI only when one of those scenarios arises. Document review? Sure. Issues list from an SPA? Absolutely. But everything else continues exactly as before - the same processes, the same bottlenecks, the same way of practising law that hasn't materially changed in decades. Use cases are the perfect on-ramp. The problem is when lawyers treat them as the destination. This is the classic faster horse problem. When Henry Ford asked people what they wanted, they said a faster horse. They couldn't conceive of the car because they were trapped in the mental model of what already existed. And that is exactly what is happening in law right now. We are retrofitting old ways of working onto a technology that demands an entirely new operating model. We're trying to bolt a jet engine onto a horse-drawn carriage and wondering why it doesn't fly. My time in practice When my previous firm rolled out Legora, I threw myself into it - not tentatively, not with a list of approved use cases, but completely. My mindset was simple: whenever a new piece of work came in, I would assume that the platform could help. I would open it before I even knew how I was going to use it. I wasn't deterred when it took time to figure out the right approach. I treated every task as an opportunity to push the boundaries of what was possible. Within months, Legora was the first thing I opened in the morning and the last thing I closed at night. It wasn't a tool I reached for occasionally. It was my legal operating system: the place where all of my work lived, where every document, every matter, every piece of context was connected and accessible. People in practice would often come up to me and ask: what are your prompts? Can you share your use cases? And of course I would, but if we're having a prompt-sharing exercise, we are in danger of missing the point. AI is changing how much that staffing advantage matters, giving mid-sized firms new ways to put their existing expertise to work. Sonia Menon said the discussions cover client questions, new use cases, cost, risk, and repeatability. As Menon described it, the partners leading those client conversations are also helping shape how the technology is introduced across the firm. blogs.content: Product Inside the Pillar Two Tax AI Assistant From PwC and Harvey Research the OECD rules and local Pillar Two legislation in one place, with a tool already used by thousands of PwC professionals. by Harvey Team • Nov 17, 2026 More than 8,000 multinational groups are in scope of Pillar Two, the OECD framework that sets a 15% global minimum effective tax rate for groups with consolidated revenue of €750 million or more. According to the OECD, 45 jurisdictions have already taken steps to introduce the Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) rules. The framework is global, but implementation is local. Those local differences decide what a group files, when it files, and how much top-up tax it owes. For tax teams, two challenges stand out. The first is data . GloBE calculations generally start from each entity's financial accounts, as prepared for the parent's consolidated statements, and then require jurisdiction-specific adjustments. Some domestic regimes may substitute consolidated statements with local accounts. Working out exactly what data each country's rules require, and whether a group's data supports it, is often the hardest part. The second is interpretation . The OECD rules don't settle every local nuance, so teams must read the global rulebook alongside each country's legislation. PwC and Harvey built the Pillar Two Tax AI Assistant , a specialist research tool within Harvey, to address both challenges. What the Assistant Covers and How it Works The Pillar Two Tax AI Assistant’s research capabilities help teams apply the global rules to local law. It covers the OECD Pillar Two rules alongside country-specific material supplied by PwC network firms, and it currently spans 21 countries. The assistant draws only on vetted public sources: enacted and draft local legislation, tax authority guidance, and other official publications such as government consultations. Online sources are refreshed weekly, new documents are added monthly, and the content is reviewed quarterly. Users select it as a source in Harvey, filter by the countries they need, and use it alongside Harvey's other platform features. It can also power custom agents that produce dashboards to help teams test and reconcile the underlying data. The custom Harvey Agent, described below, is one example. What the Assistant Does for Tax Teams Pillar Two is complex, varies by country, and constantly changes. The assistant gives tax teams a single, trusted place to work through it. Faster cross-border research. Users no longer need to search legislation and guidance country by country. They can work through filing obligations, deadlines, and country-specific requirements in one place. "The module significantly improves the efficiency of my day-to-day Pillar Two work by helping me quickly navigate filing obligations, deadlines, and jurisdiction-specific requirements," said a PwC Senior Associate, International Tax, Japan. Side-by-side country comparisons. Users can see how countries have implemented the rules and spot differences early. "The module provides quick, well-structured overviews and access to relevant guidance and legislation, making country-specific research more efficient and effective," noted a PwC Manager, International Tax, Germany. Analysis of a group's own facts. Users can upload a group's facts to see what data the rules require. They can also explore scenarios that might change the top-up tax payable, or test whether simplifications or safe harbours could apply. Research through to deliverable. The assistant drafts memos on the rules, on elements of the effective tax rate calculation, and on safe harbours and exclusions. It also helps users check their analysis and prepare reports and emails. Cited, verifiable answers. blogs.content: Insights Planning Your Law Firm’s 2027 Technology Budget by Megan McMillin • Nov 16, 2026 Preparing a law firm’s technology budget means working through requests that serve different purposes. Some spending keeps the firm’s existing systems reliable. Other investments help a practice take on new work or develop a service for clients. The firm also needs to decide how much it can spend testing ideas whose value it has yet to establish. The Three Horizons framework offers a useful comparison. It describes how organizations can support their core business while developing emerging opportunities and exploring future possibilities. Applied to technology budgeting, it helps explain why a system replacement and an experiment need different justifications. Both need a clear purpose, but the firm cannot expect the same level of certainty from each. 1. Connect spending to the firm’s priorities The firm’s plans give context to individual technology requests. A corporate practice expecting more transactions may need to reduce the time lawyers spend preparing first drafts. A new practice may need specialist research sources. Understanding the work behind a request makes it easier to assess its importance and explain why it deserves funding. Those requests sit alongside existing contractual commitments and the cost of keeping core systems operating securely and reliably. Finance, technology, and practice leaders need a shared view of those obligations when they discuss what the firm can take on next. Dependencies also affect the decision. A new knowledge tool may require the firm to organize its documents and correct access permissions before lawyers can use it effectively. The proposal needs to account for that work. Otherwise, the firm risks approving a purchase without funding the conditions that would make it useful. For each significant request, the budget discussion should establish what the firm expects to improve and what would happen if it waited another year. That gives leaders a practical basis for comparing proposals that address different needs. 2. Reassess existing tools before renewing them A complete view of technology spending includes central IT purchases, tools that practice groups buy directly, and subscriptions that individuals expense. Looking across those purchases can reveal overlapping costs or capabilities the firm already owns. Usage data helps, but it needs context. A product with few users may serve a small practice doing important specialist work. The lawyers who rely on it can explain what it contributes and what they would need instead. Low adoption can also reflect a training problem rather than a lack of demand for the tool. Contract timing matters when the firm identifies something it could replace. If an existing contract runs through September, a replacement that starts in January will create a period when the firm pays for both. The budget needs to reflect that overlap and any migration costs. Renewal notice deadlines therefore deserve attention before the firm counts on savings. The relevant number is the amount the firm can actually stop spending during the budget year, after accounting for the cost of the transition. 3. Budget for the work required to implement the technology The vendor’s price will not cover everything the firm needs to contribute. A project may require document migration, integration with other systems, and work on permissions. The budget should distinguish the services the vendor provides from the work the firm will handle itself. Internal time deserves particular attention. An AI rollout may depend on the same IT and knowledge teams that are already working on a document management upgrade. Each project can look manageable on its own. Looking at them together may reveal that the firm expects the same people to do more than they can realistically take on. That should affect the budget decision. blogs.content: Technical Building Ethical Wall Enforcement Into Harvey How we bring a firm’s matter restrictions into document access, search, and AI work. by Shuaiwei Cui , Lilly Xia , and Nick Howlett • Nov 13, 2026 Imagine a lawyer using Harvey to analyze documents for Acme Corporation’s confidential acquisition. A colleague is barred from accessing information about the deal. That restriction must also apply to conversations and other work created from those documents, even if someone shares the work with the colleague. Law firms organize work around matters, such as a deal, lawsuit, or advisory engagement. An ethical wall, also called an information barrier, limits who can access information about a matter. An inclusionary wall allows access only to people on its list; an exclusionary wall blocks the people on its list and allows everyone else in. Bringing ethical walls into an AI platform means protecting information wherever it is used. Firms manage matter records and wall policies in their own systems, and Harvey imports them. A document management system (DMS) enforces walls on the documents it stores. But Harvey also creates conversations, tables, and drafts from those documents. Because that work lives in Harvey, our platform must enforce the walls on it too. To do that, Harvey links resources — including Vault projects and files, conversations, and Review Tables — to Client Matters and their walls. This creates three engineering challenges: Import matters and walls reliably, at the scale of a large firm Help people find the matters they can access Enforce walls the same way across different kinds of work The rest of the blog explains the architecture Harvey uses to carry each firm’s ethical wall rules across the platform, from the matter model to the safeguards around wall data. Figure 1. Harvey imports matters and walls from firm systems. On every request, it checks both resource permission and matter clearance. Importing Client Matters and Walls Before Harvey can enforce a wall, it needs the matter and its policy. Our import architecture separates matter identity from access policy. Provider adapters translate data from each wall provider into one common model. Each firm’s data stays in its own workspace, the firm’s private Harvey environment. Two separate sync jobs We split import into two jobs. Client Matter sync finds matters in the external system and links each one to an existing Harvey Client Matter or creates a new one. When walls are enabled, it can also set up the matter’s wall. Wall sync refreshes the policy for matters already linked to the external system. It fetches each matter’s current policy, matches the people on it to Harvey users, applies membership changes, and updates whether the matter is open or walled. We keep these jobs separate for three reasons: Each job can run on its own schedule. A firm opens new matters at a steady pace, but a wall can change at any moment, for example when a lateral hire arrives with a conflict. Wall sync can run on demand without a scan of the full matter catalog. A failure in one job does not block the other. If a wall fetch fails for one matter, matter import continues. If matter import stalls, existing walls still refresh. Firms do not have to adopt both at once. Matter data and wall data often live in different systems. A firm can bring its matters into Harvey before it turns on walls, or without walls at all. For supported integrations, Client-Matter-only sync links an imported document collection to its matter in Vault, even if the firm has not set up walls in Harvey. blogs.content: Insights An MSA Review Should Test the Liability Cap Against Your Smallest, Riskiest SOW An MSA review sets the liability cap for SOWs you haven’t signed yet. See the three terms to test and how Harvey takes the first pass on an MSA. by Harvey Team • Nov 9, 2026 A master services agreement (MSA) sets the legal terms for a commercial relationship. Each statement of work (SOW) signed under it adds the scope, deliverables, and fees for one project. An MSA review is the legal review of those master terms before signature, and because SOWs usually inherit them, it also sets the rules for SOWs nobody has drafted yet. Take a hypothetical MSA your company is about to sign with an IT services provider. SOW-1 for implementation ($1.2 million) and SOW-3 for support ($300,000, billed annually in advance) are signed with the MSA. SOW-2, a $40,000 migration of customer personal data, follows four months later. All figures in this example are illustrative. Ten months after the MSA is signed, partway through SOW-2, a breach exposes the migrated customer data and leads to a $2 million claim against the provider. Whether the cap limits that claim to $40,000 or leaves room for all of it turns on a few words in the MSA's limitation of liability. Those words get settled during the MSA review, months before SOW-2 is written. We’ll follow this MSA from the provider’s first draft to the SOW-2 signature and show where legal AI helps. Harvey takes the first pass, finding the cap, precedence, and survival terms and comparing them with your playbook, so counsel’s time goes to the terms that decide the claim. The Cap Definition Decides Whether a $2 Million Claim Gets Limited to $40,000 The provider's draft caps its liability at the fees paid or payable under "the applicable SOW" in the 12 months before the claim. That reads as standard until you run it against SOW-2, the smallest SOW and the one carrying customer data. Here’s how far the same $2 million claim could go under three hypothetical cap wordings, assuming the cap is the only limit in play: Cap wording in the MSA (hypothetical) Cap Upper limit on the $2 million claim under this cap Fees under the applicable SOW (the provider's draft) $40,000 $40,000 Fees under all SOWs $1,540,000 $1,540,000 Fees under all SOWs, plus a data super-cap of the greater of $1 million or 3 times those fees $4,620,000 (3 times fees) for data protection claims $2,000,000, since the cap sits above the claim The provider’s draft lands at the bottom because the riskiest SOW carries the smallest fees. Counting fees under all SOWs, plus a data super-cap, puts the limit above the full claim. Harvey can do this reading for counsel. With the draft MSA, the SOWs signed alongside it, and the team’s executed MSAs in Vault, a review table lines up the cap wording against each SOW’s fees and against the cap positions the team has accepted before, each answer linked to its source. Counsel sees how small the cap gets on a low-fee, high-risk SOW before negotiation starts. A weak cap in the MSA carries into every SOW signed under it, which is why the cap sits near the top of any contract review checklist . blogs.title: Find Every Auto Renewal Clause in Your Portfolio Before its Notice Window Closes
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: An auto renewal clause can set a notice deadline months early. Sort contracts by renewal mechanism, map 30 to 180-day windows, and give each one an owner.
blogs.content: Insights Find Every Auto Renewal Clause in Your Portfolio Before its Notice Window Closes An auto renewal clause can set a notice deadline months early. Sort contracts by renewal mechanism, map 30 to 180-day windows, and give each one an owner. by Harvey Team • Nov 6, 2026 An auto renewal clause, also called an automatic renewal clause, extends a contract for another term unless a party gives notice by a set deadline. Tracking that deadline on one agreement is simple. A portfolio multiplies the deadlines, and Zylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index found that the average organization manages 211 SaaS renewals annually, before IT services and facilities agreements are counted. Take a hypothetical in-house team with about 400 supplier agreements across SaaS, IT services, and facilities. In this example, 260 of them renew automatically on January 1 unless someone gives notice. Their notice periods run 30, 60, 90, or 180 days, so the deadlines fall anywhere from July 4 to December 1. Reading 400 agreements for the same few renewal facts is the slow part, and AI can take it on. Harvey's review tables pull each agreement's renewal terms into columns linked to the source clause, so the team's time goes to checking those facts and deciding what to renew. We'll follow this team from sorting its contracts to getting each owner's decision in before the notice deadline. An Auto Renewal Clause Extends the Term Unless Someone Gives Notice in Time An automatic renewal clause sets four facts to capture: the renewal term, the notice period, who can give notice, and how notice must be delivered. Here's a sample clause from one of the team's agreements, a $240,000-a-year analytics subscription, written for this example: "This Agreement will renew automatically for successive twelve (12) month renewal terms. Either party may prevent renewal by giving the other written notice of non-renewal at least sixty (60) days before the end of the then-current term. All notices must be delivered to the addresses set out in Section 14.2." Read as data, it gives a 12-month renewal term, a 60-day notice period, a right either party holds, and a delivery rule that points to Section 14.2. A contract auto renewal clause often splits those facts across sections, so the notice address may sit in a general notices clause or in a later amendment. Missing any one of them can leave a notice of non-renewal open to challenge. The Renewal Mechanism Decides Whether Silence Keeps a Contract or Ends it Before any date matters, each contract needs a label for what happens if nobody acts. An auto renewal contract keeps running on silence, while an option to renew lapses on silence, so the two call for opposite actions. Here's how the team's 400 agreements sort, with all counts hypothetical: Renewal mechanism What happens if nobody acts Who has to act, and by when Agreements in this example Automatic renewal for a fixed term The contract renews for the stated renewal term The party that wants out, by giving notice of non-renewal before the notice deadline 300, including the 260 that renew on January 1 Evergreen, terminable on notice The contract keeps running, often month to month, until someone ends it The party that wants out, by giving notice that takes effect after the notice period 45 Option to renew The contract expires at the end of its term The party holding the option, by exercising it before its deadline 25 Fixed expiry The contract ends on its stated date Both parties, by signing a new agreement or an extension before that date 30 Some lawyers use "evergreen clause" for any automatic renewal, and others reserve it for contracts with no fixed renewal term, as the table does. Whichever label your team uses, record what silence does, since that decides whether a contract has a deadline to watch. The rest of this example follows the 260 January 1 renewals. blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: A new Harvey capability that connects facts across millions of documents to their sources, so teams can build work product on a record that grows with the matter.
blogs.content: Product Introducing Harvey’s Fact Graph for Disputes, Litigation, and Investigations The Harvey fact graph helps disputes, litigation, and investigations teams find and connect facts across millions of documents and build on one evolving record. by Harvey Team • Nov 5, 2026 We’re introducing Harvey’s fact graph, a new capability for disputes, litigation, and investigations teams to find and connect facts across millions of documents. It links those facts to supporting sources, to one another, and to the people, events, and issues they concern—helping teams uncover relationships across the full record over the lifetime of a matter. The fact graph is the newest addition to Harvey Graph , the connected map of legal knowledge and matter context that Harvey’s agents draw on to find the right information, cite it, and carry it forward. From Individual Facts to a Strategic Narrative In litigation and investigation matters, the job is to connect thousands of facts into a strategic narrative: who knew what and when, whether accounts hold up against the evidence, and where the record has gaps. The facts of a matter often seem disconnected, and the work requires ongoing resources to comb through huge volumes of information. An email might show that an executive received a warning about a defect. Meeting notes months later might record their approval of a product launch despite knowledge of the defect. Extracting and connecting those facts helps teams trace actions, assess what the evidence supports, and identify what still needs to be established. Harvey’s fact graph makes those connections across millions of documents, so teams can focus on judgment instead of piecing together the record. It extracts facts from each document, links back to the exact line of text, and connects events across the record, even when related facts seemingly appear disconnected or sit years apart. As new documents are added over time, the fact graph extracts new information, connects it to the existing record, and flags inconsistencies. New evidence or research can fill a gap, challenge an earlier account, or reveal the significance of a detail found months before. Each new document adds to what the team already knows, and the record grows with the matter. Turn Connected Facts Into Work Product Keeping the factual record current is just the foundation. Teams can also carry those facts into chronologies, witness outlines, memos, and reports. Instead of manually updating work product, Harvey keeps the context up-to-date and flags where prior work is outdated. With the fact graph, teams build work product on the same evolving record throughout the life of a matter. Agents in Harvey draw on the facts and connections already established to generate first drafts, from witness interview outlines early in an investigation, to deposition memos as evidence builds, to preparation materials for a hearing or trial. Each stage builds on the team’s accumulated understanding, so no one has to reconstruct the factual context for each new task. Build on Prior Work as Your Matter Progresses Matters can run for years, outlasting the teams that first worked on them. New team members join, responsibilities shift, and new counsel may come in just weeks before trial. Getting up to speed often means reviewing documents again, piecing together earlier analysis, and relying on handoff conversations to understand what the team knows and why. The fact graph keeps the matter’s facts, supporting sources, review decisions, and work product together, so understanding persists through every phase of the matter. Incoming teammates or counsel can easily trace the audit log, see how the team assessed earlier information, and identify inconsistencies. Every member of the team has a starting point that reflects months or years of accumulated work, so they spend less time reconstructing the matter and more time preparing for what comes next. blogs.content: Product More Specialized, More Personalized: Announcements From Harvey FORUM Chicago At Harvey FORUM Chicago, the product keynote showed how Harvey is bringing deeper context and more tailored solutions to legal teams. by Harvey Team • Nov 5, 2026 Today is Harvey FORUM Chicago, bringing together more than 500 leaders from law firms, in-house legal teams, and the legal ecosystem for candid conversations about how AI is changing legal work. During the product keynote, we shared how Harvey is driving the next phase of AI in legal work forward: more personalization to your team and organization’s ways of working and deeper specialization into practice areas. Here’s a closer look at what’s coming to Harvey. Context Will Take Legal AI to the Next Level of Value Harvey co-founder and CEO Winston Weinberg opened the keynote with a prediction for 2027: legal AI moving from a tool you prompt to a team that you run. Getting there depends on two things: agents that know a matter or project as well as its lawyers do and firms that can govern those agents with confidence. The first is a context problem. Today, many prompts start cold — a lawyer gathers the documents, explains the background, and clarifies every preference. That’s workable for a chat assistant, but it breaks down the moment agents need to carry a matter from one step to the next or when multiple lawyers and agents are collaborating on the project. That’s what Harvey Graph is built for. It maps the relationships across a firm or team’s matter or project, so agents share a map of the work instead of rebuilding it at every step. This shared context is what helps make teams of legal agents and more sophisticated output possible: they can only hand work to one another if they understand it the same way. Read about the Harvey Graph to learn how we’re improving agent accuracy . “ Think about the best manager you've ever had. They gave you proactive guidance on what to do and context on how to do it. That's what we’re building into our agents: context and control, so they operate the way you and your team do every step of the way. ” Winston Weinberg Co-Founder and CEO at Harvey iManage: Two-Way Sync to Your System of Record For many of the firms in the room, context about a matter begins in iManage. Shawn Misquitta, who leads product at iManage, joined Winston to talk about what our teams are building together next and the value for shared customers. The main takeaway? Read-only access isn't enough. Harvey and iManage have built a two-way integration that will be in early access soon. Context flows into Harvey, finished work flows back to iManage, and iManage remains the system of record. The ethical wall policies your firm already maintains in iManage carry over and are enforced in Harvey. Three ways Harvey Will Get More Personalized and More Specialized Harvey’s Chief Product Officer, Anique Drumright shared how Harvey is becoming more personalized for how your teams serve the business and specialized to what your practice area needs. Outlook: Harvey Where You Already Work Harvey agents are now in Outlook, giving you a legal AI assistant inside the inbox and calendar you already live in, tailored to exactly how you work. Here’s a look at what the agent can do: Triage and filing : Sort incoming email by matter or deal and file attachments to the right Vault, so your day starts organized instead of with cleanup. Drafting and scheduling : Drafts replies and propose resolutions to scheduling conflicts without leaving the thread. Work that kicks off from email : Suggest and start first-pass review when a new draft lands, pulling in context from your firm’s connected systems. Agents you build yourself : A personal daily briefing agent can triage your inbox overnight so the summary is waiting when you start your day. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.225 → v2.1.233 3 features · August 10–14 Auto-continue after a usage limit on Desktop Desktop When you hit your session limit in the Code tab of Claude Code Desktop, the limit card now offers an Auto-continue when limits reset checkbox. Check it, and the Desktop app retries the interrupted turn after the reset. The card shows the retry time. The weekly-limit card doesn’t offer it. The next time a session-limit card appears, check Auto-continue when limits reset and leave the session open. The card shows Auto-resuming at followed by the reset time, and the turn picks up on its own once the limit resets. What to do when you hit a usage limit Fork mode on by default v2.1.232 Fork mode is now on by default in interactive sessions. Claude can request the fork subagent type, which inherits the full conversation and prompt cache instead of starting fresh, so you don’t have to re-explain the context for a side task. Subagents Claude spawns in interactive sessions, apart from the ones an agent-team teammate spawns, also run in the background by default. Start a fork yourself with a task that needs everything you’ve discussed so far: Claude Code > /subtask draft unit tests for the parser changes so far The fork appears in the panel below your prompt and its result arrives in your conversation when it finishes. To turn fork mode off, set CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 . Turn fork mode on or off GitLab merge requests and marketplaces v2.1.232 Plugin marketplaces clone bare gitlab.com URLs, including nested subgroups. On v2.1.233 or later, pass a GitLab merge request URL to --worktree to branch from it, and the claude agents view labels sessions linked to a merge request as !N . blogs.description: Law firms are hiring for AI fluency. Learn the five levels firms expect, how to show your level on a resume and in interviews, and how to reach the next.
blogs.content: Insights AI Fluency in Legal Hiring and How to Show it “Comfortable with AI tools” in a job description tells candidates very little. Instead, firms can offer a common scale for AI fluency that shows students and junior lawyers what firms expect, and gives them a way to prove themselves fluent. by Peter Duffy • Nov 5, 2026 AI fluency is fast becoming a hiring priority for law firms. It means knowing how to use AI effectively in legal work, recognize its limitations, and apply your own judgment to its outputs. For students thinking about recruitment, that raises a practical question: What exactly do firms want students to know regarding AI, and how do you show you’ve got it? A few firms are leading the way with clarity around expectations. One recruitment post I came across recently opened with a single question: “Are you a lawyer who builds?” The post didn't come from a legal tech start-up or an alternative legal service provider, but a newly launched AI-forward practice set up by a leading European law firm. To explain what it meant, the firm pointed candidates to Levels 4 and 5 of Harvey’s recently published AI Fluency Framework : Builders , who create reusable AI tools such as agents and playbooks, and Catalysts , who build for others and set the standards around them. From AI Familiarity to Clear Expectations A few years ago, it would have been unusual to see law firms recruit explicitly for Builders and Catalysts. In the case of the aforementioned recruitment post, the firm made it clear that it needs lawyers who create with AI, not just use it, and it used the framework's levels to outline their expectations. This example shows how the ideal candidate profile has changed and what law firms are looking for specifically — not just an introduction to AI but the ability to build agents and think critically about how and when to use AI, pointing to a clear framework to attain and measure those skills If firms and candidates share a common language for AI fluency, the framework works just as well at the hiring stage as it does for a junior lawyer in development inside the firm. A firm built around AI is likely to be a step ahead of the wider market, but its hiring expectations are an early sign of where recruiting is heading, and quickly. Among the most progressive firms, AI fluency is already a skill set in rising demand. Expectations are getting clearer — and higher. For students, that makes it worth understanding those expectations now, before they become the norm. The Problem With "Comfortable With AI Tools" Look beyond the most AI-forward employers, and the picture is less precise. Many legal job descriptions mention AI in some form: "comfortable with AI tools," "tech-savvy," "keen interest in legal innovation." These phrases signal a firm's intent, but they set a tone without setting a bar. Comfortable doing what? Using AI to summarize a contract, identify key obligations, and check the summary against the source? Using AI to analyze deposition transcripts, identify inconsistencies, and verify findings against the record? Building an agent that teammates or a practice area can rely on, with clear instructions and review steps? Spotting where AI could reshape how a whole team works, then guiding changes to workflows and working practices? These are very different levels of fluency. Today every role can benefit from a clear standard, and for most lawyers that standard should be Proficient : regular, confident use of AI on substantive legal work. Where firms need Builders or Catalysts, being specific matters even more. The same clarity helps throughout a lawyer's career. A shared standard gives interviewers a consistent way to assess AI capability, gives development plans a clear destination, and shows both current and future lawyers what their goals should be, how to develop, and what their next step looks like. What's missing is a common reference point: a shared understanding of what's expected, where the baseline sits a

blogs.author: AutoClaw Team
blogs.description: AI 能几秒写出理财产品营销文案，但流畅不等于准确。本文从事实核验、产品事实底稿、客户问题任务单、人工复核到 30 天小规模试点，讲财富管理机构如何用 AI 提升内…
blogs.content: 返回博客 AI理财产品营销内容创作：如何兼顾内容效率与事实准确性 资讯 作者：AutoClaw Team 2026年11月17日 AI 能几秒写出理财产品营销文案，但流畅不等于准确。本文从事实核验、产品事实底稿、客户问题任务单、人工复核到 30 天小规模试点，讲财富管理机构如何用 AI 提升内容效率，同时守住产品信息与风险提示的准确性。 每一次写作工具的进步，最先改变的往往不是思想，而是文字来到我们面前的方式。生成式 AI 将这种速度推到了一个新的位置。只需一个题目、一段要求和几份资料，文字便像早已等候在门外，迅速走到我们面前：一篇产品解读、一段渠道摘要、一张海报的标题，几乎同时有了雏形。 然而，当写作越来越快，金融内容里那些缓慢的东西反而显出了分量。一个数据需要找到出处，一处省略需要还原语境，一句关于收益与风险的表达，需要有人停下来，重新读一遍。本文讨论 AI 生成理财产品营销内容时，如何通过事实底稿、人工复核与流程管控，在内容效率与事实准确性之间取得平衡。 想象一个普通的傍晚。一位财富管理机构的内容编辑收到三项任务：把同一款理财产品分别写进公众号文章、App 产品页和客户经理问答。窗外的天色渐暗，屏幕上的文档却迅速增多。AI 已经完成了初稿，句子完整，语气妥帖，甚至带着一种令人放心的确定。但编辑的工作并没有结束。她仍要回到产品资料里，确认那组业绩属于哪个区间、那项费用对应什么条件，也要判断标题中的“稳健”，究竟是产品事实，还是语言制造出的错觉。 一款理财产品走进 AI 的叙述，只需要几秒钟；让这段叙述经得起事实与责任的追问，却需要一条更长的路。 一、AI 生成理财产品营销文案为什么越流畅越需要事实核验 语言有一种不易察觉的能力：它会掩盖信息之间的接缝。当产品名称、投资策略、历史业绩与配置价值被组织进一个自然段，读者很容易因为行文顺畅，而默认这些信息同样真实、同样完整。AI 生成内容的风险，恰恰藏在这种“读起来没有问题”的时刻。 最难发现的错误，往往不是荒诞的数字，而是恰到好处的偏移。“近一年”没有写明截至日期，便失去了确切的时间边界；业绩比较基准被改写成“预期收益”，一个用于理解产品运作的参考指标，便可能被误认为对未来的许诺；一段历史业绩之后紧跟着“未来值得期待”，叙述便从产品记录悄悄滑向了对明天的暗示。 有些偏移还藏在产品的差异里。公募基金的不同份额可能对应不同费用安排，银行理财产品的期限、开放规则与流动性约束也各有具体要求。若改写时只保留最有吸引力的部分，读者看到的便不再是一款完整的产品，而是一幅经过裁切的轮廓。这些句子并不喧哗，也不需要夸张的承诺。它们只是少了一个条件，换了一个语境，或者在两处真实信息之间，搭起了一座并不存在的桥。 因此，AI 生成理财产品营销文案的第一项要求，不是让语言更审慎，而是让事实能够被核验。产品名称、识别信息、费用、风险等级、期限与开放安排、业绩区间和数据日期，都应能回到批准使用的资料；找不到来源的内容，不应因为表达自然而获得豁免。 流畅是一篇文章的外表，可追溯才是它站稳的地方。 二、AI 理财产品营销内容为什么要从产品事实底稿开始 如果把 AI 生成内容比作水流，产品事实底稿便是河床。它不决定文字最终会呈现出怎样的波纹，却决定文字不会流向哪里。 事实底稿不是把产品合同、说明书、定期报告、运作公告和历史文案堆进同一个文件夹。资料越多，并不等于方向越清楚。真正可用的底稿，需要有人提前完成选择、确认和标注：哪些资料现行有效，哪些数据可以使用，哪些信息只适用于特定产品类别、份额或渠道。 它至少要讲清一款理财产品的几个基本侧面： 它是谁：产品全称、管理或发行机构、产品类型与适用的识别信息； 它如何运作：投资目标、投资范围、主要策略、期限与开放安排； 它可能经历什么：风险等级、主要风险因素，以及收益和本金可能受到的影响； 它涉及哪些成本与限制：认购、申购、赎回、管理等费用，以及适用的持有或流动性安排； 它过去发生了什么：历史业绩、业绩比较基准及相关数据的来源、统计区间、截至日期与比较口径。 不同产品不能机械地共用同一张底稿。公募基金需要区分份额，银行理财可能更需展开期限与开放安排，其他产品也各有必须保留的要素。真正可以共用的是来源管理和核验原则，而不是一套完全相同的产品字段。 底稿中还应留下事实的来路。每一项关键信息，都应尽可能携带来源文件、数据日期、适用范围和审核状态。这样，当同一事实被写进不同渠道时，编辑不必重新在文件中寻找它，审核人员也能迅速确认它是否被正确使用。 一份事实底稿的价值，不在于让内容显得厚重，而在于让每一次轻盈的改写都有落脚处。当资料无法回答一个问题时，流程也应当允许 AI 停笔。标记缺失、退回补充，远比生成一个看似完整的答案更重要。涉及收益、费用和日期的关键数据，则应使用经过验证的结果，而不是依靠模型临时推算。 三、理财产品营销团队如何用客户问题为 AI 内容确定方向 每一位读者来到一篇理财产品文章之前，都带着自己尚未解开的疑问。 有人看到产品名称中的“稳健”，便以为净值不会下跌；有人把业绩比较基准理解为未来可以拿到的收益；也有人面对几款名称相近的产品，不知道该从哪些相同口径开始比较。还有人已经持有一段时间，翻开定期报告或运作公告，却难以分辨哪些变化值得理解，哪些数字只是时间长河中的一次涟漪。 如果内容任务只有一句“介绍这款理财产品”，这些具体的疑问就会被覆盖。AI 很可能交出一篇结构完整的产品介绍，却没有真正走近任何一个人。更好的起点，是先写出读者的问题，再决定产品的哪些事实应当被引用。 面对刚接触某一产品类型的读者，文章可以先解释收益从哪里来、风险为什么存在；面对正在比较不同产品的读者，内容可以提供风险等级、投资范围、期限、费用与流动性等观察维度，同时说明比较所需的一致口径；面对持续关注产品的持有人，则更适合回到定期报告和运作信息，帮助读者理解产品运作中的变化。 同一个事实底稿，由此可以生长出不同的内容，而不是复制出不同长度的广告。这要求营销人员在生成前写清一张任务单：内容发布在哪里，写给哪类读者；读者已经知道什么，还可能误解什么；本篇只回答哪一个核心问题；允许使用哪些资料；哪些产品要素、数据口径与风险提示必须保留。好的内容任务，不是让 AI 把卖点说得更响亮，而是让它帮助团队把一个问题讲得更明白。文字的方向，仍来自人对读者的理解。 四、AI 生成理财产品宣传内容为什么必须保留人工复核 金融内容里有些判断，无法被简化成词语检查。例如一句“它经受住了市场的考验”，即使紧接着一段真实的历史业绩，也仍值得追问：所谓“考验”指哪一段市场环境？产品当时的回撤、波动与流动性安排是否同时呈现？这段经历为什么能够支持当前表述？标题是否让读者对尚未发生的事情产生了过度确定的理解？ 人工复核的意义，就是在内容发布之前，补回那些被省略的部分。一套可落地的AI理财产品营销内容流程，可沿七个节点展开：先确认资料准入，再按产品类型建立事实底稿；由营销人员建立内容任务单，AI生成候选初稿；随后逐项完成事实一致性检查，进入机构要求的专业审核；发布后，还需在产品资料、管理信息、费用、开放规则或风险信息发生变化时，定位并处理受影响的内容。 其中，产品名称、识别信息、类别或份额、数字、日期、费用及期限安排，都应能从初稿映射回事实底稿。查无来源的句子应被删除或退回，而不是通过润色保留下来。业务人员需要检查产品理解，合规人员按照机构制度完成必要审核，渠道负责人则要看清标题、摘要和展示位置是否改变了正文原意。 不同类型理财产品适用的发布规则和审核要求并不完全相同。流程可以复用，审核标准不能简单套用。AI 可以承担检索辅助、版本对比、渠道改写和缺项提醒，但产品判断、语境判断、适当性边界与最终发布决策，仍应由具备相应职责的人完成。 五、财富管理机构如何用小规模试点衡量 AI 内容的真实价值 当 AI 进入内容团队，最先增长的往往是文档数量，而不一定是有效产能。 如果初稿从每天两篇增加到十篇，审核退回、事实核对与渠道返工也随之增加，那么速度只是从一个环节转移到了另一个环节。真正需要衡量的，是一篇内容从任务发起到最终发布，究竟消耗了多少人的时间，又留下了多少可避免的错误。 因此，小规模试点比全面铺开更能说明问题。团队可以选择少量产品和一至两个高频渠道，用 30 天完成一次验证： 第 1 周，盘点资料与历史问题。**选择具有代表性的产品类型，整理现行资料、常见事实错误和内部审核要求，保留人工生产的对照样本。 第 2 周，建立事实底稿与内容任务单。**按产品类型确定字段、来源记录和更新责任，明确资料缺失时的处理方式。 第 3 周，开展小批量人机协同。**生成候选初稿，记录每一次人工修改的原因，而不只统计生成耗时。 第 4 周，复盘审核与更新机制。**确认哪些字段必须逐项复核、哪些情况必须退回，以及产品信息变化后由谁触发存量内容更新。 试点结束时，值得放在一起比较的，不只是篇数，还包括单篇内容实际工时、首次审核通过率、平均返工轮次、事实差错率，以及信息变化后定位和处理存量内容所需的时间。 阅读量、留资量与转化率仍然重要，但不宜全部记在 AI 名下。渠道位置、市场环境和投放资源都会改变结果。AI 内容项目首先需要证明的，是在质量要求不降低的前提下，团队是否减少了重复劳动，内容是否变得更容易核对与更新。 回到那个傍晚。 编辑最终发布的，或许仍是三篇篇幅不同、语气不同的内容。但在它们背后，产品事实来自同一份经过确认的底稿，每个关键数字都能回到出处，每一次删改也留下了人工判断的痕迹。 AI 并没有失去它的速度。只是速度不再独自决定文章的去向。 一款理财产品的名字

blogs.content: Week 28 · July 6–10, 2026 Copy page Copy page Browse external sites from the Desktop app’s built-in browser, run a full setup checkup with /doctor, and pick up auto mode transcript protections and agent view upgrades. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.202 → v2.1.206 2 features · July 6–10 In-app browser on Desktop Desktop Claude Code on desktop now has a built-in browser. Claude can pull up docs, designs, or any other site, and read, click through, and interact with pages the same way it does with your local dev server previews. The browser is sandboxed and configurable: you choose whether browsing sessions persist, and safety classifiers review actions on external sites. Browse external sites /doctor is a full setup checkup v2.1.205 /doctor now diagnoses issues and can fix them, instead of printing a read-only report. It checks installation health, finds unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost, deduplicates local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones, proposes trimming CLAUDE.md content Claude could derive from the codebase, and flags slow hooks. It reports findings first and asks for confirmation before changing anything. /checkup is its alias. Run a checkup from any session: Claude Code > /doctor All commands Other wins Auto mode now blocks tampering with session transcript files, and asks before running rm -rf on a variable it can’t resolve from context /cd now suggests directory paths as you type, matching /add-dir /commit-push-pr auto-allows git push to the repo’s configured push remote in addition to origin Gateway: /login now supports Anthropic-operated public gateway endpoints EnterWorktree asks for confirmation before entering a git worktree outside the project’s .claude/worktrees/ directory Background agents upgrade to a new version in the background right after a Claude Code update, instead of paying a slow stale-session upgrade when you attach Agent view rows now show a colored state word and a classifier-written headline instead of raw tool call text, and sessions that edit, merge, comment on, or push to an existing PR link it in claude agents Auto-update binary downloads now stream to disk instead of buffering in memory, cutting the updater’s peak memory usage by roughly 400 MB Background task notifications now explicitly state that no human input has occurred, preventing fabricated in-transcript approvals from being acted on Improved /code-review findings quality on Opus 4.8 across all effort levels Full changelog for v2.1.202–v2.1.206 → Was this page helpful? blogs.content: Week 26 · June 22–26, 2026 Copy page Copy page Authenticate MCP servers from your shell with claude mcp login, get a response to shell mode command output with the ! prefix, and resume a conversation from before /clear with /rewind. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.185 → v2.1.193 2 features · June 22–26 Authenticate MCP servers from the CLI v2.1.186 New claude mcp login <name> and claude mcp logout <name> commands authenticate a configured MCP server from your shell instead of the interactive /mcp menu. claude mcp login runs the server’s OAuth flow directly, and claude mcp logout clears the stored credentials. Run the OAuth flow for a configured server without opening a session: terminal claude mcp login sentry Authenticate from the command line Shell mode responds to command output v2.1.186 Commands you run with the ! prefix now get a response from Claude once the output lands in the transcript, so you can run ! npm test and get an explanation of the failures without a second prompt. The response costs the same as sending a normal prompt. To keep the earlier behavior, where the output is added to context without a response, set respondToBashCommands to false in settings.json . Run a command and get a response to its output: Claude Code > ! npm test Shell mode with the ! prefix Other wins /rewind can now resume a conversation from before /clear was run New sandbox.credentials setting blocks sandboxed commands from reading credential files and secret environment variables Org-configured model restrictions now apply to the model picker, --model , /model , and ANTHROPIC_MODEL , with a “restricted by your organization’s settings” message when a restricted model is selected New autoMode.classifyAllShell setting routes all Bash and PowerShell commands through the auto-mode classifier, and denial reasons now show in the transcript, the denial toast, and /permissions New claude_code.assistant_response OpenTelemetry log event carries the model’s response text; deployments that already log prompt content start receiving it on upgrade, so set OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=0 to keep prompts only Background subagents now surface permission prompts in the main session instead of auto-denying; the dialog shows which agent is asking, and Esc denies only that tool /install-github-app can now install only the GitHub App and skip the Actions workflow and secret steps Hosts you allow in the sandbox network permission dialog are remembered for the rest of the session instead of re-prompting on every connection Streaming responses use about 37% less CPU, and long-session memory growth from the terminal output cache is reduced /review <pr> now uses the same review engine as /code-review medium Bash mode ! commands get live file path autocomplete Full changelog for v2.1.185–v2.1.193 → Was this page helpful? blogs.content: Week 25 · June 15–19, 2026 Copy page Copy page Publish a live, shareable page from your session with Artifacts, match tool parameters in deny and ask rules, and set any setting from the prompt with /config. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.178 → v2.1.183 3 features · June 15–19 Artifacts An artifact is a live, interactive page that Claude Code publishes from your session to a private URL on claude.ai, and it updates in place as the session keeps working. Ask for one when terminal text is the wrong medium, such as a PR walkthrough with the diff annotated inline or a dashboard built from session data. Artifacts are in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Ask Claude for a page, then approve the publish prompt: Claude Code Make an artifact that walks through this PR with the diff annotated inline. Create an artifact Match by input parameter v2.1.178 Deny and ask permission rules can now match a tool’s input parameters with the Tool(param:value) syntax. For example, Agent(model:opus) matches subagent spawns that request the Opus model tier. The value accepts * as a wildcard, so Agent(isolation:*) matches any explicit isolation value. Add a parameter rule to the deny list in settings.json : .claude/settings.json { "permissions" : { "deny" : [ "Agent(model:opus)" ] } } Match by input parameter Set any setting from the prompt v2.1.181 Pass key=value to /config to change a setting directly without opening the Settings interface. The syntax also works in non-interactive mode with the -p flag and from Remote Control. Set the thinking setting from the prompt: Claude Code /config thinking=false Commands reference Other wins Auto mode now blocks destructive git commands ( git reset --hard , git clean -fd , git stash drop ) when you didn’t ask to discard local work, and blocks terraform destroy unless you asked for the specific stack Set the new attribution.sessionUrl setting to false to omit the claude.ai session link from commits and PRs in web and Remote Control sessions In the /config interface, Enter and Space both change the selected setting, and Esc now saves and closes instead of reverting New sandbox.allowAppleEvents opt-in setting lets sandboxed commands send Apple Events on macOS Point CLAUDE_CLIENT_PRESENCE_FILE at a marker file to suppress mobile push notifications while you’re at the machine Long paragraphs now stream line by line instead of waiting for the first line break API connection drops mid-thinking now retry automatically instead of showing “Connection closed while thinking” With CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 set, every session has one implicit team, so you spawn teammates directly with the Agent tool’s name parameter Skills in nested .claude/skills directories load when working on files there; on a name clash the nested skill appears as <dir>:<name> so both stay available Fixed prompt caching not reading on a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and on Microsoft Foundry Fixed Write and Edit producing zero-byte or truncated files on network drives and cloud-synced folders Full changelog for v2.1.178–v2.1.183 → Was this page helpful? blogs.content: Week 24 · June 8–12, 2026 Copy page Copy page Move a session to a new directory with /cd, let subagents spawn their own subagents, and troubleshoot a broken configuration with safe mode. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.166 → v2.1.176 3 features · June 8–12 Move a session with /cd v2.1.169 The new /cd command moves the current session to a different working directory without rebuilding the prompt cache: the new directory’s CLAUDE.md is appended as a message instead of replacing the system prompt. The session relocates to the new directory’s project storage, so --resume and --continue find it there. Claude prompts you to trust the directory if you haven’t worked in it before. Move the session into another project without restarting: Claude Code > /cd ../other-project Commands reference Subagents can spawn subagents v2.1.172 Subagents can now spawn their own subagents. The subagent panel below the prompt shows the full tree: each row carries a count of its descendants and a path back to main . Subagent chains are capped at five levels deep to prevent runaway concurrent trees. Open the agents view to watch the nested tree as work fans out: Claude Code > /agents Spawn nested subagents Troubleshoot with safe mode v2.1.169 Start Claude Code with --safe-mode , or set CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE , to launch with all customizations disabled: CLAUDE.md , skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, and custom commands and agents do not load. Authentication, model selection, built-in tools, and permissions still work. If a problem disappears in safe mode, one of those surfaces is the cause. Launch a clean session to isolate a broken configuration: terminal claude --safe-mode Test against a clean configuration Other wins fallbackModel configures up to three fallback models tried in order when the primary is overloaded or unavailable, and --fallback-model now applies to interactive sessions too Session titles are now generated in the language of your conversation; pin a specific one with the language setting claude agents --json adds --all to include completed sessions plus new id and state fields, and no longer omits blocked or newly dispatched sessions Browsing a marketplace’s plugins in /plugin now has a search bar New disableBundledSkills setting and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BUNDLED_SKILLS hide bundled skills, workflows, and built-in commands from the model Deny rules accept a glob in the tool-name position, so ”*” denies all tools, and unknown tool names in deny rules now warn at startup Agent messaging is hardened: messages relayed via SendMessage from other agents no longer carry user authority, and auto mode blocks them Amazon Bedrock reads the AWS region from ~/.aws config files when AWS_REGION is unset, and /status shows where the region came from New enforceAvailableModels managed setting makes the availableModels allowlist also constrain the Default model Claude in Chrome browser tools now load in a single batched call instead of one per tool claude update announces the target version before downloading instead of going silent New footerLinksRegexes setting adds regex-matched link badges to the footer row Full changelog for v2.1.166–v2.1.176 → Was this page helpful? blogs.content: Week 23 · June 1–5, 2026 Copy page Copy page Run auto mode on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, prompt before writing files that can run code in acceptEdits mode, list installed plugins with /plugin list, and require an approved version range for managed deployments. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.158 → v2.1.165 4 features · June 1–5 Auto mode on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry v2.1.158 Auto mode is now available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry for Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8, replacing permission prompts with background safety checks on third-party providers. Opt in by setting CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE=1 . Opt in on a third-party provider, then cycle to auto mode with Shift+Tab: terminal export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE = 1 Auto mode on third-party providers Safer automatic edits v2.1.160 Claude Code now prompts before writing files that can run code, even in acceptEdits mode. The protected set covers shell startup files such as .zshenv and .bash_login , git config under ~/.config/git/ , and build-tool configs such as .npmrc , .bazelrc , and .pre-commit-config.yaml . These writes are never auto-approved in any mode except bypassPermissions . Work in acceptEdits mode; Claude now pauses before writing these files: terminal claude --permission-mode acceptEdits Protected paths List installed plugins with /plugin list v2.1.163 The new /plugin list command prints your installed plugins inline, without opening the /plugin menu, and is also available as claude plugin list from the shell. In the interactive form, add --enabled or --disabled to show only plugins in that state. List the plugins that are currently turned on: Claude Code > /plugin list --enabled Plugin commands Version requirements for managed deployments v2.1.163 Two managed settings, requiredMinimumVersion and requiredMaximumVersion , let your organization require an approved Claude Code version range. A client outside the range exits at startup and tells the user to update through the organization’s method. claude update , claude install , and claude doctor keep working so users can still recover. Add a floor to your managed settings so older clients refuse to start: managed-settings.json { "requiredMinimumVersion" : "2.1.163" } Decide what to enforce Other wins The trigger keyword for dynamic workflows changed from workflow to ultracode ; asking for a workflow in your own words still works, and the keyword is highlighted in violet in the prompt Stop and SubagentStop hooks can return hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext to give Claude feedback and keep the turn going instead of being treated as an error claude mcp list, get, and add no longer print secrets: environment-variable references are not expanded, and credential headers and URL secrets are redacted A failed Bash command in a parallel tool batch no longer cancels the others; each tool returns its own result independently Editing a file no longer needs a separate Read first when you viewed it with a single-file grep , egrep , or fgrep Clicking a command in the autocomplete menu now fills it into your prompt instead of running it immediately; press Enter to run Listing Grep or Glob in --tools now provides the dedicated search tools on native builds with embedded search, instead of silently ignoring those names /effort now confirms when your chosen level will persist as the default for new sessions OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES values are now attached as labels on metric datapoints, so you can slice usage metrics by custom dimensions like team or repo Windsurf is renamed to Devin Desktop in /ide , /terminal-setup , and /scroll-speed , following the editor’s rebrand /btw gains a c to copy shortcut that copies the raw markdown answer to the clipboard Full changelog for v2.1.158–v2.1.165 → Was this page helpful? blogs.author: Kimi
blogs.description: 基于 Kimi K3.1 系列模型、Kimi Code 与 Kimi Work 系列 Agent 产品，以及 Unity、Unreal Engine、Blender 等专业工具插件，帮助游戏团队更快验证玩法创意、推进工程和美术制作，并将发行与运营中的玩家反馈带回下一轮迭代。
blogs.content: Kimi 发布游戏开发与创意工作解决方案 联系销售团队 下载 Kimi 桌面端 今天， Kimi 发布「游戏开发与创意工作解决方案」。 基于 Kimi K3.1 系列模型、Kimi Code 与 Kimi Work 系列 Agent 产品，以及 Unity、Unreal Engine、Blender 等专业工具插件，我们希望帮助游戏团队更快验证玩法创意、推进工程和美术制作，并将发行与运营中的玩家反馈带回下一轮迭代。 游戏创意的价值，往往要到玩家真正操作时才能判断： 策划文档能说明规则，却难以回答操作是否顺手、奖励是否明确、节奏是否吸引人。若这些问题在关卡、代码和资产大量完成后才暴露，调整就会牵动更多人和预算。 Kimi 希望帮助团队尽早做出范围明确的可玩版本，再根据真实体验决定如何投入。 游戏行业的业务挑战：更快验证，也要稳定交付 游戏开发的第一道门槛，是创意验证的成本 。 一个玩法是否有趣，需要真正玩起来才能判断。但制作原型需要投入时间和人力，团队往往只能优先验证少数想法。如何降低单次尝试的成本，在有限时间内验证更多创意？ Unity《2026 Game Development Report》 显示，52% 的受访开发者优先选择小规模项目来降低风险，67% 将原型阶段控制在三个月以内。更审慎的研发投入、更紧凑的验证周期，让原型制作效率变得更加重要。 Kimi 游戏解决方案，可以帮助游戏团队高效制作项目原型，在有限时间内探索和比较更多玩法方向，从而做出更准确的业务判断。 第二道门槛，来自跨岗位和跨工具的协作 。策划需求，需要变成工程任务；美术资产，也需要符合引擎规范。AI 若只生成一段文字或一张图，仍需要团队花大量时间进行适配和创作，才能搬进原有流程。 Kimi 解决方案可以直接衔接团队现有的工作流，操作专业工具与编辑器、修改现有工程，并交付可继续编辑的文件和清晰的操作记录，方便团队审阅、协作和推进后续工作。 Kimi 游戏开发与创意工作解决方案：从创意落地到持续迭代 Kimi 可以从团队的实际目标出发，推动创意从设想走向实践。 例如，策划想验证「在三消玩法中加入可自由组合的规则卡」是否有趣，但仅凭玩法说明，很难感受规则叠加后带来的策略变化。Kimi 会围绕这一目标，梳理规则卡的组合方式及其对消除策略、得分与反馈的影响，再将其拆解为交互、数值、界面和视听等具体制作任务，制作可试玩的原型。 这样，策划、开发和美术就能围绕同一个原型，边玩边讨论，减少创意在沟通与交接中的理解偏差。 结合模型能力与专业工具，Kimi 还可以将这种工作方式的变化，延伸到游戏开发、制作等更多环节。 模型能力与插件支持 一个游戏项目往往横跨多个团队，涉及策划文档、截图、代码、3D 资产等多种项目文件。 Kimi 可以为这一复杂流程提供支持：模型负责理解这些输入并规划、执行任务； Kimi Code 支持面向代码库中的实现和修改； Kimi Work 可以承接跨文件、跨步骤的制作任务。团队可以在这些成果的基础上继续完善，衔接后续制作流程。 针对不同团队的需求，我们也提供了覆盖日常办公、代码开发与 API 集成的系列产品，供大家选择： 此外，Kimi 还可通过插件与工具调用连接 Blender、Unity、Unreal Engine 等专业软件，直接操作现有工程，协助完成游戏开发与 3D 创作等任务。 正式立项前：用 Godot 把想法做成可试玩原型 游戏立项前，团队往往需要快速验证新玩法，但开发资源未必充足。 借助 Kimi，缺少编程经验的策划或创意团队也能在 1–2 天内做出可试玩原型。先验证玩法，再决定是否投入。 比如，团队想制作一款 2.5D 动作游戏的原型，可以提供参考图和视频，说明预期的场景氛围与玩法机制。Kimi 通过多模态能力理解参考素材中的关键视觉元素，再使用 Godot 游戏引擎搭建可试玩 Demo，呈现雨夜光影、地面积水和灯笼等场景细节，并实现挥剑、闪避和格挡等核心玩法。 制作过程中，Kimi 还可以实际运行游戏，结合渲染画面和试玩录像，检查视觉效果与功能是否达到要求。发现问题后，自主修改并重新验证，在交付前完成多轮迭代，让团队拿到的首个版本更接近预期。 有了可试玩原型，团队就能围绕实际体验展开评审：雨夜中的战斗辨识度、挥剑打击感，以及闪避与格挡的攻防体验。 团队可以据此不断调整和复测，验证核心玩法是否成立，再决定是否扩展关卡与敌人类型。 美术资产适配：让 Blender 资产从概念走向游戏场景 美术资产进入游戏场景，要经过比概念呈现更严格的检查：角色多视角是否一致，模型有无穿插，纹理和隐藏文字是否有缺陷，资源规格能否满足引擎预算。 Kimi 可以协助完成上述检查与初步调整：模型通过多模态理解，结合多视角视频与截图判断空间关系，发现并定位比例、穿插和材质问题；再将调整方案转化为脚本，借助本地 Agent 操作专业软件，完成初步修改。 通过 Blender 插件，Kimi 可以直接操作软件，协助美术团队搭建、预览和修改场景。 团队既可以提供现有工程与资产，让它完成摆放、组合和布局调整；也可以提供参考图片或视频，附上制作要求，让它从零建模、组装资产并搭建场景，还原参考中的整体形态与空间布局。 以建筑场景为例，根据美术团队提供的资产或参考图片及制作要求，Kimi 会在软件里先确定建筑的整体形态与空间布局，再逐步完善结构、材质和灯光；复杂建筑则拆分为不同构件，分步搭建与细化。搭建过程中，通过多视角预览检查模型比例、穿插与材质表现，及时发现并修正问题，提升首版交付的完成度与质量。美术团队可在此基础上继续打磨，把握最终风格与质量，将更多精力投入设计判断与细节表现，减少基础搭建和反复排查的工作量。 Kimi K3.1 Pro 使用 Blender 构建了一座机场室内雨林山谷场景，并制作了一段 17.5 秒、1920×1080 分辨率、60 fps 的 3D 建模展示视频。使用工具：Blender、Python、Geometry Nodes（几何节点）、Cycles（渲染引擎）、Pillow、NumPy 和 FFmpeg。使用的外部素材：来自 Poly Haven 的 4K HDRI 环境贴图 “Kloofendal 48d Partly Cloudy (Pure Sky)”，由 Greg Zaal 和 Jarod Guest 创作，采用 CC0 许可协议，用于天空照明和环境反射。 Kimi K3.1 Pro 在 Blender 中构建了一个可交互的、基于浏览器的 3D 体验，打造了一座大教堂的内部场景。该场景约包含 330 万个三角面，并为 8,368 个组件制作了动画效果，呈现出肋拱穹顶、石雕塑像，以及色彩鲜明的彩绘玻璃光影。使用的外部素材：来自 Poly Haven 的石材纹理（CC0 许可）；Mylius 拍摄的彩绘玻璃照片（CC BY-SA 3.0 许可）。 游戏开发：把 Agent 带入 Unity 与 Unreal Engine 的现有工程 进入正式开发后，团队面对的是已有工程、既定架构和不断变化的需求。 一个看似简单的功能，可能同时影响角色状态、界面、存档和关卡逻辑；一个完整的 3D 场景，也要兼顾空间关系、视觉效果、物理交互与运行性能。工程越复杂，模块之间的依赖越多，问题就越难定位和解决。 面对这类牵一发而动全身的工程问题，Kimi 可以在获得工程文件和必要权限后，先梳理代码结构、场景层级和模块依赖，找到真正需要修改的位置，再借助插件在 Unity、Unreal Engine 等编辑器中完成具体操作。 改动完成后，Kimi 会结合问题复现、日志和运行数据验证效果，并根据结果继续调整。交付时保留代码差异和验证记录，方便工程师检查功能、性能与兼容性。 围绕这套工作流程，我们在内部探索了几类用法： Kimi + Unity：从网页试玩走向专业开发。 可玩 Demo 只是开始，要走向正式上线，还需进一步完善工程，以支撑后续的调试、打磨与持续迭代。Kimi 模型与 Unity 中国推出的游戏开发智能体 Tuanjie Codely Agent 及 团结引擎协同 ，将需求理解、工程实现与测试迭代串联起来：Kimi 模型负责理解开发者的创作意图与游戏设计、生成实现代码，并根据录屏与测试结果分析问题、制定修改方案；Tuanjie Codely Agent 则依托与团结引擎的原生整合，通过 Editor / Runtime Script 等方式直接在引擎中执行操作，完成场景搭建、玩法实现、工程修改与运行验证。 开发流程由此从“人提需求—模型写代码—人来操作”，延伸为“模型理解与生成—Agent 操作引擎—模型分析反馈—Agent 修改工程并验证”的完整闭环，减少了开发者在工具间切换与手动操作的成本。 在一次演示中，Kimi 在没有人工干预的情况下连续工作 20 小时，不仅复现了原作，还产出了一份可持续开发的原生工程，为后续玩法扩展、画面打磨及多端适配打下基础。 Kimi + Unreal Engine：跨模块的玩法开发与联调。 游戏玩法的新增或调整，往往会同时牵动角色行为、动画、物理效果和界面反馈。开发者提供相关脚本、组件配置与预期效果后，Kimi 可以梳理各模块之间的调用关系，协助修改代码、补充日志与测试，并结合 Unreal Engine 中的实际表现进行联调。以古风武侠游戏中的“处决”玩法为例，玩家靠近敌人后，角色需要连贯完成拔剑、攻击和收剑动作，并触发后续剧情。Kimi 可以协助完成人物动作绑定、模拟处决后的物理效果、衔接战斗与剧情逻辑，排查动作错位、倒地异常或剧情未
